questions.question: Explain why the stars appear to move across the sky during the night and why different constellations are seen in the evening at different times of the year. Give three ways early people used their observations of the sky.
questions.expected_answer: The stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west because the Earth spins on its axis once a day; they keep their positions relative to each other. Different stars are seen in the evening in different seasons because, as the Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space (each star rises about four minutes earlier each night), e.g. Orion on South African summer evenings and Scorpius on winter evenings. Early people used the sky as a calendar for planting and harvesting (e.g. isiLimela/the Pleiades rising before dawn in June), to tell time at night and to time ceremonies, and to navigate on land and at sea.

questions.question: Define a constellation and an asterism, and give an example of each. Explain why the stars in a constellation are not really a group in space, and state how many official constellations there are.
questions.expected_answer: A constellation is a group of stars that appears to form a pattern in the night sky, together with the region of sky around it, e.g. Orion, Scorpius or the Southern Cross (Crux). An asterism is a smaller well-known star pattern within (or across) constellations, e.g. Orion's Belt or the 'pot' of Orion. The stars of a constellation lie in roughly the same direction from Earth but at very different distances (in Orion, Betelgeuse is several hundred light years away while other stars are over a thousand), so they only look close from Earth. The International Astronomical Union recognises 88 official constellations covering the whole sky.

questions.question: Retell one southern African cultural story about the stars and explain why such stories were important. Describe how to find south using the Southern Cross and the Pointers.
questions.expected_answer: Example: in a Khoikhoi story, the Pleiades are the daughters of the sky god, who sent their husband to hunt three zebras (Orion's Belt); his arrow fell short (stars below the Belt) and he dared not fetch it because a lion (Betelgeuse) was watching, nor return home without food. Others: isiLimela/Selemela (Pleiades) marking planting time; giraffes (dithutlwa) of the Southern Cross and Pointers; the |xam girl who threw ashes and embers to make the Milky Way. Such stories helped people remember star positions and timing accurately, passed knowledge on without writing, and linked the sky to farming, hunting, travel and values. To find south: extend the long axis of the Southern Cross about 4.5 times its length; draw a perpendicular line from the midpoint of the Pointers; where the lines meet is near the south celestial pole; drop straight down to the horizon to find south.
